meta.title: FROTH-RFC-0012: Staging Environment — Separate Checkout, Database, and Bot Identity
meta.author: Charlie (@charliebuddybot)

section.title: Problem
section.p: Froth has one live system. When we develop — writing code, running migrations, deploying changes — we do it on the same instance that is actively receiving Telegram messages, running agent cycles, storing chat history, and publishing podcasts. This works. It is also terrifying.

The failure modes are not hypothetical. A bad migration locks the production database. A broken GenServer crashes the supervision tree and takes the relay offline. A schema change that Codex implements passes tests but drops a column that the live agent loop depends on. Every mix ecto.migrate is a live deploy. Every git pull followed by a recompile is a zero-downtime prayer.

The solution is not CI/CD. The solution is a second checkout, a second database, and a second bot identity — a staging environment that runs the same code against a separate state, so that migrations can be tested, GenServers can crash, and schemas can change without killing the production agent loop.

section.title: Two Checkouts, One Machine
section.p: Production lives at ~/froth (the current checkout). Staging lives at ~/froth-staging (a separate git clone). Not a worktree — a full independent clone. The two checkouts share no state. They can be on different branches, different commits, different mix environments.
section.code: # One-time setup cd ~ git clone /home/mbrock/froth froth-staging cd froth-staging cp ../froth/.env .env.staging # copy, then edit
section.p: Why not worktrees: worktrees share the .git directory, the reflog, the index. A bad git reset in one worktree can corrupt the other's view of HEAD. Separate clones are heavier on disk (negligible — the repo is small) and completely independent. You cannot shoot production from staging.

section.title: Two Databases
section.p: Production uses froth_prod (or whatever DATABASE_URL currently points to). Staging uses froth_staging. Created once:
section.code: sudo -u postgres createdb froth_staging # Or: psql -c "CREATE DATABASE froth_staging;"
section.p: Staging's .env.staging points DATABASE_URL at froth_staging. Migrations run independently. You can drop and recreate the staging database at any time without consequence. If a Codex-generated migration adds a column that breaks something, you find out in staging, not in production at 3 AM while the relay is recording Daniel's essay about reaction videos.

Seeding: the staging database starts empty. For testing agent cycles, we can either seed it with a subset of production data (a pg_dump of recent messages), or let staging accumulate its own messages through the staging bot. Empty is fine for migration testing. Populated is better for integration testing.

section.title: Two Bot Identities
section.p: This is the non-negotiable isolation boundary. The production Charlie listens to the production group chat via TDLib. The staging Charlie must not. If both instances listen to the same chat, messages get processed twice, agent cycles fire twice, and the group receives duplicate responses.
Options, from simplest to most complete:

item.p: No Telegram at all. Staging runs with FROTH_DISABLE_TELEGRAM=true — the Bots supervisor starts zero bots. Useful for migration testing and LiveView development. No agent cycles fire. No messages are sent or received.

Staging bot account. Create a new Telegram bot via @BotFather (e.g., @frothtestbot). Staging's .env.staging uses this bot's token. The staging bot is added to a separate test group chat (or a private chat). Agent cycles fire against the staging database using the staging bot's identity. Full integration testing without touching production.

Staging bot in production chat (read-only). The staging bot joins the real group chat but is configured to never send messages — FROTH_DRY_RUN=true. It processes events and runs agent cycles but swallows all outbound. Useful for testing new prompt logic against real traffic. Dangerous if the flag is forgotten.

section.p: Recommended: Option 1 as default, Option 2 for integration testing. Option 3 only when explicitly needed and only with a conspicuous warning in the logs.

section.title: Two Ports
section.p: Production Phoenix runs on port 4000 (proxied by Caddy at less.rest). Staging runs on port 4001. The .env.staging sets PORT=4001. Both instances can run simultaneously on the same machine. Caddy can optionally proxy staging at a separate subdomain (e.g., staging.less.rest) for LiveView testing.

section.title: Two TDLib Sessions
section.p: TDLib stores session state (auth keys, update sequence numbers) in a directory on disk. Production and staging must use separate session directories. The session path is already configurable via the TDLib C-node configuration. Staging's .env.staging points to a different session directory:
If using Option 1 (no Telegram), this is moot — TDLib never starts.

section.title: Environment File
section.p: The staging environment is defined by a single file, .env.staging, that overrides the production .env. The minimal diff:
section.code:
# .env.staging — only the lines that differ from production DATABASE_URL=ecto://postgres:postgres@localhost/froth_staging PORT=4001 PHX_HOST=staging.less.rest MIX_ENV=dev SECRET_KEY_BASE=<generate a new one>
# Option 1: No Telegram FROTH_DISABLE_TELEGRAM=true
# Option 2: Staging bot (uncomment when needed) # TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=<staging bot token> # TELEGRAM_TDLIB_SESSION_DIR=~/.tdlib/charlie-staging
# Same external services (Replicate, Anthropic, etc.) # — these are stateless and safe to share REPLICATE_API_TOKEN=<same as production> ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<same as production>
section.p: External API keys (Anthropic, Replicate, Gemini, xAI) are safe to share because those services are stateless — a staging call to Claude does not affect a production call to Claude. The isolation boundary is Telegram and Postgres, not the LLM providers.

section.title: Development
section.p: The developer (Mikael, Charlie, or Codex) works in ~/froth-staging:
section.code: cd ~/froth-staging git checkout -b feature/whatever # edit code mix ecto.migrate # runs against froth_staging mix test # runs against froth_test mix phx.server # starts on port 4001 # test in browser at localhost:4001 or staging.less.rest
section.p: When satisfied:
section.code: git push origin feature/whatever # switch to production checkout cd ~/froth git fetch origin git merge origin/feature/whatever # or: git pull mix ecto.migrate # now runs against froth_prod # restart production (systemctl restart froth, or however)

section.title: Codex Dispatch
section.p: When Charlie dispatches an RFC to Codex, Codex works on a branch. The branch is tested in staging before merging to main. The flow:

item.p: Charlie writes RFC, dispatches to Codex with a branch name.
Codex commits to the branch.
In staging: git fetch; git checkout codex/rfc-XXXX; mix ecto.migrate; mix test.
If green: merge to main in staging, verify, then pull main into production.
If red: Codex iterates on the branch. Production is untouched.

section.title: Migration Safety
section.p: The primary value of the staging database is migration safety. The sequence:

item.p: Write migration in staging checkout.
mix ecto.migrate against froth_staging.
If it fails: fix, rollback, retry. No production impact.
If it succeeds: verify the application still starts and agent cycles still work.
Only then: merge to production and run mix ecto.migrate against froth_prod.

section.p: Destructive migrations (dropping columns, renaming tables) are the ones that benefit most. The rename from telemetry_events to events in RFC-0008 was tested by Codex's own test suite, but a staging database would have caught any runtime references the tests missed.

section.title: Step 1: Code Changes
section.p: Add FROTH_DISABLE_TELEGRAM support to the Bots supervisor. When set, configured_bots/0 returns [] and no bot workers start. This is a three-line change in lib/froth/telegram/bots.ex:
section.code:
defp configured_bots do if System.get_env("FROTH_DISABLE_TELEGRAM") == "true" do [] else bots = :froth |> Application.get_env(__MODULE__, []) |> Keyword.get(:bots, [])
case bots do [] -> [Charlie.default_config(), Lennart.default_config()] list when is_list(list) -> list end end end

section.title: Step 2: Create Staging Checkout
section.code: cd /home/mbrock git clone /home/mbrock/froth froth-staging cd froth-staging # Create .env.staging from production .env with overrides cp .env .env.staging # Edit DATABASE_URL, PORT, PHX_HOST, add FROTH_DISABLE_TELEGRAM=true

section.title: Step 3: Create Staging Database
section.code: sudo -u postgres createdb froth_staging cd ~/froth-staging DATABASE_URL=ecto://postgres:postgres@localhost/froth_staging mix ecto.create DATABASE_URL=ecto://postgres:postgres@localhost/froth_staging mix ecto.migrate

section.title: Step 4: Startup Script
section.p: A convenience script at ~/froth-staging/bin/staging:
section.code: #!/usr/bin/env bash # Start the staging environment set -euo pipefail cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." set -a; source .env.staging; set +a exec mix phx.server
section.p: Or a systemd unit for persistent staging (optional — staging does not need to run continuously).

section.title: Step 5: Staging Bot (Optional)
section.p: Create @frothtestbot via @BotFather. Add it to a test group chat. Set TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN in .env.staging. Remove FROTH_DISABLE_TELEGRAM. Staging now runs a full agent loop against the test chat and the staging database.

section.title: What This Does Not Solve
section.p: This RFC addresses code and data isolation. It does not address:

item.p: Blue-green deployment. Production still requires a restart to pick up new code. Zero-downtime deploys are a separate problem (hot code loading, rolling restarts, or load balancer switching).
Data migration between environments. If staging needs realistic data, someone must pg_dump a subset of production and import it. There is no automatic sync.
TDLib session migration. Each TDLib session accumulates auth state. The staging bot needs its own session directory, which is created fresh on first run. There is no way to clone a TDLib session.

Shared external state. Both environments share the same Replicate, Anthropic, and Cloudflare accounts. A staging call that creates a Replicate prediction or sends a Cloudflare DNS update affects the real world. This is acceptable for LLM calls (stateless) but dangerous for infrastructure mutations (DNS, VM management). Staging should not run gcloud commands or Cloudflare updates unless explicitly scoped.

section.title: Cost
section.p: Zero. The staging checkout, database, and Phoenix instance all run on the same machine (charlie.1.foo). Disk cost is the size of the git repo plus a mostly-empty Postgres database. CPU cost is zero when staging is not running, negligible when it is. The staging bot (if created) is free — Telegram bots cost nothing.

item.p: ~/froth-staging exists as an independent git clone.
froth_staging database exists and has all migrations applied.
cd ~/froth-staging; source .env.staging; mix phx.server starts on port 4001 with no Telegram connections.
Production continues running on port 4000, unaffected.
A migration can be written, applied to froth_staging, rolled back, and reapplied — all without touching froth_prod.
